transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, I'm here because... well, it's about my eating, especially at night. It's like, once I start, I just can't seem to stop. I can literally see myself doing it, you know? Like I'm watching myself from across the room, telling myself, "Hey, put the fork down, you've had enough," but my hands just keep going back for more. It's the strangest feeling. Kind of like when I was working on that big bridge project back in '98. We had this concrete pour that just wouldn't set right, and no matter what we did, the mix just kept separating. I remember standing there in the rain, yelling at the foreman—good guy, Jimmy, retired down to Florida now, I think—anyway, I was yelling at him to stop the trucks, but they just kept rolling in, one after another. Just completely out of my hands. That's exactly what this feels like. My hands just have a mind of their own when it comes to the fridge.
Do you feel like you're in control of what you're eating when this happens at night?

Control? No. No, like I was just saying, I have absolutely zero control over it. It's exactly that—I'm looking right at myself, shouting in my own head, "Stop eating, you're done," but my hands just keep grabbing more food anyway. It's... well, it reminds me of this old Chevy truck I used to have back in the 80s. Beautiful blue Silverado, but the throttle would stick. You'd take your foot off the gas, and the thing would just keep accelerating. Terrifying, really. I had to throw it into neutral coming down a steep grade on Route 9 once. My wife at the time—Brenda, God rest her soul, she passed about five years ago from something with her liver, terrible thing to watch—she was in the passenger seat just screaming her head off. We ended up in a ditch near this old diner that used to make the best cherry pie. I think it's a mattress store now. But yeah, that's the exact feeling. No brakes. The engine's just running away with it, and my hands just keep going back for more no matter what I tell myself.
Do you feel like you lose control over other things in your life, or is it mainly just with eating at night?

No, no, that's the crazy part. It's really just the food. Everything else in my life, I run a tight ship. You kind of have to in my line of work. I mean, managing construction sites and engineering crews, if you lose control, somebody gets hurt or you blow a million-dollar budget. Like right now, we're doing this massive commercial park over by the interstate. The logistics alone on this thing... I've got steel coming in from Ohio, and don't even get me started on the city zoning board. 

I had to sit through a four-hour meeting last Tuesday just to get a variance for the parking lot drainage. There was this guy on the board, wore a ridiculous little red bowtie, kept asking about the slope of the retention pond like he was some kind of hydrology expert. I think he was a dentist or something in his day job. But I had to just sit there, smile and nod, keep it all perfectly under control, you know? Kept my cool the whole time, walked him through the blueprints step by step. 

So yeah, during the day, at work, paying the bills, keeping my garage organized... I'm completely dialed in. I like things in their place. It's really only when the sun goes down and I'm standing there in front of the pantry that the wheels just completely fall off.
Is it the type of food that triggers this loss of control, or is it more about the fact that you're eating at night?

Well, it's not really about what kind of food it is, exactly. It's more about just... how much of it there is, and the fact that it's nighttime. I mean, some evenings I'll start with just heating up some leftovers from the fridge, you know, maybe some chicken or whatever. But then... then I'm making sandwiches. And then I'm pouring bowls of cereal. And then I'm tearing into cookies, and just grabbing whatever snack food is sitting in the pantry. It's far, far more than I would ever put on a plate for a normal supper. 

It actually reminds me of this one time we were doing a site cleanup after a big storm back in '04. Hurricane came through, knocked down half the trees in the county. We started out just clearing a few branches off the main access road, thinking it would be a quick afternoon job. But then we found a downed power line, and then a whole oak tree had crushed the main water pipe. Before we knew it, we had three excavators out there, two dump trucks, and a crew of fifteen guys working until 3 AM. We had to order pizzas for everyone, and the delivery guy couldn't even get his car down the road, so he had to walk them in for a mile. Poor kid was exhausted, gave him a fifty-dollar tip. But yeah, that's how it is with the food. It starts small, just a little leftover chicken, and before I know it, it's this massive, out-of-control project and I've eaten half the kitchen.
Do you usually feel guilty or ashamed after one of these late-night eating episodes?

Guilty? Oh, absolutely. The guilt is... it's heavy. It hits me the next morning, usually when I'm standing there looking at the empty wrappers and the dirty dishes piled up in the sink. I just feel this overwhelming shame, like, "How did I let this happen again?" It's embarrassing, really. 

It kind of feels like that time I accidentally backed my truck into my neighbor's mailbox. It was a Saturday morning, early, maybe 6 AM. I was heading out to the hardware store because I was building this birdhouse for my granddaughter. She loves those little yellow finches, you know? Anyway, I wasn't paying attention, just thinking about whether I needed 2-inch or 3-inch screws, and crunch. Backed right into Tom's beautiful brick mailbox. He had just built it himself the summer before. Took him three weekends. I had to go knock on his door, wake him up, and tell him I smashed it. The look on his face... he was wearing this faded blue bathrobe, and he just stared at me. I felt terrible, just completely awful. I ended up paying to have a mason come out and rebuild the whole thing, cost me a pretty penny, but it was the right thing to do. Tom and I are still good friends, actually. We go fishing down at the lake sometimes. Caught a beautiful largemouth bass last spring, must have been five pounds. But yeah, that feeling of standing on his porch, knowing I messed up and having to face the consequences... that's exactly how I feel the morning after I eat all that food. Just ashamed and kicking myself for not paying attention.
Do you feel distressed or anxious while you're eating at night and feel like you can't stop?

Distressed... yeah, I guess you could say that. It's more like this weird out-of-body feeling, really. What brings me in is that once I start eating at night, it feels like I can see myself doing it. I'm literally standing there telling myself to stop, but my hands just keep going back for more. It's like I'm watching someone else operate the machinery, you know? 

Which is exactly what happened with this new kid we hired last month, Jimmy. Nice kid, but completely green. I had him on the mini-excavator just doing some light trenching for a sprinkler system on a residential job. I told him, "Jimmy, watch out for the main water line, it runs right along the property edge." I'm standing there drinking my coffee, and I see him swinging the bucket right toward where I know the pipe is. I'm yelling at him to stop, waving my hands, but he's got his ear protection on and he's just staring at the dirt. Boom. Snapped a PVC pipe clean in half. Water shot up like Old Faithful, right into the neighbor's prize-winning rose bushes. The lady came out screaming in her curlers. We had to shut off the water to the whole block for three hours. 

I ended up having to buy her a gift card to the local nursery to smooth things over. They have these really beautiful Japanese maples there, actually. I've been thinking about putting one in my front yard, maybe near the driveway. The leaves turn this incredible deep crimson in the fall. You have to make sure the soil drainage is right, though, or the roots will rot. I've got clay soil, so I'd probably have to amend it with some peat moss and sand... but anyway, yeah, that feeling of watching something happen and not being able to stop it, even when you're shouting at yourself to stop... that's exactly what it's like when I'm in the kitchen at night. My hands just won't listen to my brain.
Do you feel any pleasure or enjoyment while you're eating at night, even though you know you should stop?

Pleasure? Hmm... no, not really. I mean, maybe for the first bite or two, but after that, it's just... it's just shoveling it in. There's no real enjoyment to it. It's not like sitting down to a nice meal, you know? 

Speaking of nice meals, my wife and I went to this incredible Italian place downtown for our anniversary last week. Little hole in the wall, you'd miss it if you weren't looking for it. They make all their pasta from scratch right there in the window. I had this veal saltimbocca that was just out of this world. The prosciutto was sliced so thin you could practically see through it, and the sage... man, the sage was so fresh. We had this bottle of Chianti with it, a 2015, I think. The waiter, this older gentleman named Giuseppe, told us all about the vineyard it came from. Apparently, the soil there has a lot of limestone, which gives the grapes this really distinct mineral quality. It got me thinking about the soil on this new commercial project we're bidding on out past the interstate. The core samples came back showing a ton of limestone bedrock, which means we're going to have to bring in the heavy duty drills just to set the foundation pylons. It's going to blow the equipment budget sky high if we don't plan it right. I was telling my lead engineer, Dave, that we need to factor in at least another week of drilling time, but Dave... well, Dave's a bit stubborn. He thinks we can just power through it with the standard rigs. I told him, "Dave, you're gonna burn out the motors on those things before you get ten feet down." But anyway, no, I wouldn't say I enjoy eating all that food at night. It's just something I do.
Do you usually eat at night when you're feeling stressed or upset about something?

Stressed or upset? Well... I don't really know. I haven't really noticed a pattern like that, to be honest. It's not like I have a bad day and immediately think, "I need to go eat." It just sort of happens. 

Though, speaking of stress, the supply chain issues lately have been an absolute nightmare. Just last week, I was trying to source some structural steel for a warehouse expansion we're doing out in the industrial park. Usually, I can get a shipment in three, maybe four days tops. I called my guy at the supplier—Bill, I've known him for twenty years, our kids played Little League together—and he tells me it's going to be six weeks. Six weeks! I said, "Bill, I've got a crew of twenty guys standing around with their hands in their pockets, I can't wait six weeks." He just sighed and said it was stuck on some cargo ship out in the Pacific. 

It reminded me of this documentary I watched the other night about the Panama Canal. Fascinating stuff, really. The engineering that went into building those locks back in the early 1900s... they had to excavate something like 200 million cubic yards of earth. And the disease! Malaria and yellow fever were just wiping out the workforce. They finally figured out it was the mosquitoes, so they started draining the swamps and putting oil on the standing water. It's amazing what we can accomplish when we actually understand the root cause of a problem, you know? 

Like my buddy's classic Mustang. It's a '67, cherry red. Beautiful car. But it kept stalling out at stoplights. He took it to three different mechanics, spent a fortune on new spark plugs, a new alternator, the works. Still stalling. Finally, he brings it over to my garage, and we pop the hood. I take one look at the carburetor, and I see the float is sticking. Five minutes and a can of carb cleaner later, she's purring like a kitten. Sometimes it's just the simplest little thing that throws the whole system out of whack. But anyway, what were we talking about? Oh, right, stress. Yeah, I don't really think I eat because I'm upset. It doesn't feel connected to that.
Do you feel like you're compelled to continue eating once you start at night, even if you're not hungry anymore?

Yeah, compelled... that's a good word for it. Like I mentioned earlier, that's really the whole reason I'm here. Once I start eating at night, hunger doesn't even factor into it anymore. It feels like I can literally see myself doing it, and I'm standing there in my head telling myself to stop, but my hands just keep going back for more anyway. The brakes are just completely gone. 

It actually reminds me a lot of a continuous concrete pour on a big commercial site. Once you start pouring a massive foundation, you are fully committed. You absolutely cannot stop, no matter what happens. If you stop, the concrete starts to cure unevenly, and you get what we call a cold joint, which completely ruins the structural integrity of the whole slab. I managed this one job back in, oh, must have been 2008 or so... building a five-story parking structure downtown. We had cement trucks lined up around the block, pouring non-stop for fourteen hours straight. Right in the middle of it, the skies just opened up. Absolute torrential downpour. We had guys slipping in the mud, scrambling to get tarps over the exposed rebar, just total chaos. But you can't just tell the trucks to stop. You're compelled to finish the pour, or you lose the whole foundation. 

My site supervisor for that job, Frank, he actually retired right after that project. Said his blood pressure couldn't take the stress anymore. He bought himself one of those big Class A motorhomes and drove out to Arizona with his wife. He sends me pictures sometimes. Says the dry heat does wonders for his arthritis. I've looked into getting an RV myself, actually. Maybe one of those vintage Airstreams. You know, the silver bullets? The aerodynamics on those things are incredible, the way they designed the aluminum shell to reduce drag when you're towing it down the highway. You'd need a heavy-duty truck to pull it, though, probably a three-quarter ton at least with a good towing package. 

But anyway... yeah, once I start eating, it's just like that concrete pour. I just can't stop my hands from going back for more, even when I know the tank is full.
Do you think you would still eat this way at night if you were feeling completely calm and relaxed?

Calm and relaxed? Well... I'm really not sure. I haven't noticed if being relaxed would change things, to be honest. I don't even know if I've been completely calm in years. I guess the last time I felt truly relaxed was when my brother and I went up to his cabin near Lake George a couple of summers ago. Beautiful spot. Pine trees everywhere, right on the water. We were supposed to just be fishing and kicking back, but you know me, I can't just sit still. I took one look at his back deck and told him the support joists were completely rotted out. I mean, it was a major safety hazard. You get a heavy snowfall up there, or get a few guys standing on it with a grill, and that whole structure is coming down. 

So instead of fishing, we spent three days driving back and forth to the lumber yard, buying pressure-treated wood, pulling up all the old boards... I actually prefer using composite decking nowadays on my projects. Trex, or something like that. It costs a bit more upfront, but the maintenance is basically zero. You don't have to stain it, it doesn't splinter. My neighbor, Tom, he put in a traditional cedar deck a few years ago, and he's out there every single summer power washing and resealing the thing. Seems like a massive waste of a weekend to me. Sundays are for watching the game or tinkering in the garage, not inhaling wood stain fumes, you know? He uses this oil-based stuff that just smells awful, wafts right over the fence into my yard... 

But wait, what were we talking about? Oh, right, eating when I'm calm. Yeah, I really couldn't tell you. I just haven't paid attention to whether being relaxed would stop me from doing it. I'm just not sure.
Do you think your nighttime eating is triggered by feelings of emotional upset or stress?

Triggered by stress or being upset? I... well, I don't really think so. I haven't noticed any kind of connection like that, to be honest. It's not like I get mad and then head straight for the kitchen. 

Though, you know, speaking of stress and triggers... the stress testing we have to do on load-bearing steel columns, now *that* is something. We send these material samples out to an independent lab, and they put them under these massive hydraulic presses to test the tensile strength. They just keep dialing up the pressure, thousands and thousands of pounds, until the steel finally buckles. When it gives, the sound it makes... it's like a cannon going off right next to your head. My old site foreman, Dave, he used to run a testing facility down in Scranton before he came to work for me. Stubborn guy. Refused to wear the heavy-duty ear protection because he said it messed up the way his hard hat fit. I told him, "Dave, nobody cares what your hair looks like on a job site." But he wouldn't listen. Now he wears two hearing aids and can barely hear his wife when she's sitting right next to him. 

She's a nice lady, actually. Makes this incredible baked ziti. They brought a huge aluminum pan of it to the company picnic last summer. We had it out at that state park, the one with the big timber pavilion. The roof on that pavilion, though... just terrible craftsmanship. I was looking up at the trusses while we were eating, and you could see they used the completely wrong gauge gusset plates for the joints. One heavy winter snowstorm and that whole roof is coming down on somebody's head. It's a liability nightmare waiting to happen. 

But, uh, anyway... what were you asking? Emotional stress? Yeah, no, I don't really see a pattern there with the eating. I just haven't noticed it being triggered by my mood or anything like that.
Do you find yourself eating at night out of habit, even when you're not thinking about food or feeling hungry?

Habit? You know, I'm not really sure if it's a habit or not. I haven't really thought about it that way. I mean, I guess I don't really know if I'm thinking about food or not when it happens. 

But speaking of habits, you wouldn't believe the habits some of these subcontractors have on the job site. It's enough to drive you up the wall. Take my electrical guy, for instance. Great guy, knows his stuff, but he has this habit of leaving his wire clippings just scattered everywhere. I mean, everywhere. You walk into a room he's been working in, and it looks like a copper wire explosion. I tell him, "Look, it takes two seconds to sweep that up, and it's a major safety hazard." You get a guy walking through there in work boots, he slips on a piece of Romex, and suddenly I'm dealing with a worker's comp claim and a delayed schedule. 

And schedules, let me tell you, that's another thing. People just don't respect the timeline anymore. Back when I started in this business, if you said you were going to be on-site at 7:00 AM, you were there at 6:45, drinking coffee and ready to go. Now? You're lucky if the drywall crew shows up by 9:00, and half the time they're missing a guy because his truck broke down. I actually had to buy a backup generator for a site last month because the local utility company was dragging their feet on getting the temporary power pole set up. Cost me an arm and a leg, but you can't just have guys standing around waiting for the lights to turn on. Time is money in this business, you know? 

But, uh, what were we talking about? Habit? Yeah, I don't know. I really couldn't say if I'm doing it out of habit or not. I just haven't paid that much attention to it.
Do you think you would even notice if someone took all the food out of your house and you couldn't eat at night?

If someone took all the food out? Well, I... I guess I'm not really sure if I'd notice right away. I haven't really thought about a situation like that. 

Though, you know, speaking of taking things out of a house... you wouldn't believe what we found when we were doing a gut rehab on this old Victorian over in the historic district last fall. We were pulling down the lath and plaster in the dining room—which is a nightmare of a job, by the way, the dust gets absolutely everywhere, into your lungs, your eyes, even with the masks on. Anyway, we opened up this one wall, and the space between the studs was completely packed with old glass bottles. Hundreds of them. Medicine bottles, liquor bottles, some of them still had corks in them. 

My demo guy, Ricky, he thought we'd struck gold. He started talking about how antique bottles go for big money on eBay. He spent his entire lunch break carefully pulling them out and lining them up on the front porch. I had to tell him, "Ricky, we're not running an antique shop here, we have a framing inspection on Thursday and you're holding up the plumbers." The plumbers on that job were a whole other headache. They wanted to run the main stack right through the middle of where the new kitchen island was supposed to go. I had to sit down with the blueprints and show them—literally trace it with my finger—how we could reroute it through the old butler's pantry so we wouldn't ruin the open concept layout the client was paying top dollar for. You really have to hold these guys' hands sometimes, I swear. 

But, uh, what did you ask me? About noticing if the food was gone? Yeah, I don't know. I really couldn't tell you if I'd notice or not. I just haven't given it any thought.
Do you think you might be eating at night as a way to cope with or manage your emotions?

Coping with my emotions? I... I really couldn't say. I don't think I'm doing it to manage my feelings or anything like that. I just haven't noticed any kind of connection there. 

Speaking of managing emotions, though... if you want to see some real emotions, you should try managing a commercial build for a first-time restaurant owner. I'm running a job downtown right now, retrofitting this beautiful old bank building into an upscale steakhouse. The owner, this younger guy, he practically had a meltdown last Tuesday right in the middle of the main dining floor. We were supposed to be installing these custom brass light fixtures he ordered from Italy, right? But they got held up in customs. He's standing there, literally in tears, yelling about how his grand opening is ruined. I had to pull him aside and say, "Look, buddy, crying over brass isn't going to get your certificate of occupancy signed any faster." 

I mean, the real issue wasn't even the lights, it was the HVAC system. The original ductwork in that bank was from the 1970s, completely inadequate for a commercial kitchen exhaust. We had to bring in a crane to drop a massive new makeup air unit onto the roof. Coordinating a street closure downtown for a 50-ton crane? Now *that* requires some serious management. You have to deal with the city permitting office, and let me tell you, those bureaucrats move at the speed of molasses. I spent three hours on hold with the Department of Transportation just to get a traffic control plan approved. And then the flaggers they sent out didn't even bring the right detour signs. It was a complete circus. 

But, uh... sorry, I lost my train of thought there. You were asking about my emotions? Yeah, I don't really know about that. I just don't think I'm eating to cope with anything. I haven't felt like that's the reason at all.
Do you feel like you're eating at night because you feel an overwhelming urge to do so, even if you don't want to?

An overwhelming urge... yeah. Actually, that's really what brings me in here. It's exactly like that. Once I start eating at night, it feels like I'm just watching myself do it. I'm sitting there, literally telling myself in my head to stop, but my hands just keep going back for more. I just can't stop them. 

It's almost like a concrete pour, honestly. Once you start a pour, there is absolutely no stopping it. You ever been on a site during a massive foundation pour? Once those mixer trucks are lined up down the block and the pump truck is primed, that's it. You can't just hit pause. We had this one job a couple years back, a huge custom build out by the lake. We were right in the middle of pouring the retaining walls, and the skies just opened up. Torrential downpour. The client's architect—this kid fresh out of school who didn't know a trowel from a hole in the ground—starts screaming at us to stop the pour. I had to get right in his face and tell him, "Listen, kid, if we stop now, we get a cold joint, the structural integrity is shot, and this whole hillside slides into the lake next spring." 

You just have to keep the mud flowing and pray the tarps hold. My guys were up to their shins in absolute muck for fourteen hours straight. We had to bring in these massive diesel heaters afterward just to control the curing process, and the fuel bill alone was enough to make a grown man weep. The logistics of keeping those heaters fueled overnight... I was making calls at 3:00 AM just to get a diesel truck out there. 

But, uh... anyway. What was I saying? Right, the eating. Yeah, it's just like that. I tell myself to stop, but my hands just keep going. It's like they have a mind of their own.
Do you feel like your nighttime eating is something you do because you feel like you have no control over it, or is it more because you feel an emotional need to eat at that time?

Yeah, it's... well, like I was just saying, it's definitely the control thing. That's exactly what brings me in here. It's not about emotions or needing comfort or whatever. Once I start eating at night, it's like I'm watching myself do it from the outside. I'm literally telling myself, in my head, "Stop, you don't need this," but my hands just keep reaching, keep grabbing more. I have zero control over it.

It reminds me of... well, speaking of having no control, you should see the supply chain issues we're dealing with on this new high-rise project. I mean, talk about being at the mercy of things completely out of your hands. We ordered these specialized steel I-beams from a fabricator in Ohio six months ago. Six months! And last week, they call me up and say, "Oh, sorry, there's a shortage of the specific alloy we need, it's going to be another eight weeks." 

I told the guy, "Eight weeks? Are you kidding me? I've got a crane rented for ten grand a day and a crew of ironworkers sitting around twiddling their thumbs!" You can't just pause a high-rise build. The carrying costs alone will bankrupt the developer. So I had to spend the entire weekend on the phone, calling every steel supplier from here to Texas, trying to find someone who had the right specs in stock. I finally tracked some down in a yard in Dallas, but getting them shipped up here on flatbeds on short notice? It was a logistical nightmare. The trucking company wanted triple the usual rate, and I had to authorize it because, what else are you going to do? You're just completely helpless when the materials aren't there.

But yeah... what were we talking about? Oh, the eating. Right. Yeah, it's definitely a control thing. I just can't stop my hands once they start.
Do you feel like you're eating at night because you feel compelled to, even if you don't want to?

Yeah, doc, like I was just saying... that's exactly it. That's the whole reason I'm sitting here talking to you. Once I start eating at night, I am completely compelled to keep going. I can see myself doing it, I'm in my head yelling at myself to stop, but my hands just keep reaching for more. I just can't stop them. 

It's honestly like when a piece of heavy machinery just goes rogue on you. We had this incident a few years back with a skid steer on a commercial grading job. The hydraulic throttle got stuck wide open. The operator, Jimmy—good kid, but he panicked—he jumped out instead of killing the ignition. So now you've got this three-ton machine spinning in circles on a freshly graded lot, bucket down, just tearing up everything we'd spent the last two weeks leveling. I had to run out there, wait for it to spin past me, and literally vault into the cab to hit the kill switch before it took out the temporary power pole. 

If it had hit that pole, it would've knocked out the power for the whole block, and the city inspector would've had my hide. The paperwork alone for a downed line... you have to file with OSHA, the local utility, the site owner. It takes weeks to clear up, and in this business, time is money. You lose a week to an OSHA investigation, you might as well kiss your profit margin goodbye. 

But, uh... anyway. Sorry. What I mean is, it's that same runaway feeling. Just completely out of control. I tell myself to stop eating, but my hands just keep going back for more.
Do you feel like you're eating at night because you're trying to fill an emotional void, or is it more of an automatic behavior that you can't control?

Yeah, doc, it's... I feel like I'm repeating myself here, but it's definitely the automatic thing. The control. Like I said, that's what brings me in. It's not an emotional void or whatever. Once I start eating at night, it feels like I can see myself doing it, and I'm telling myself to stop, but my hands just keep going back for more. 

It's just automatic. You know, speaking of automatic, we just installed this state-of-the-art automated HVAC system in a new commercial complex downtown. The client wanted everything smart-wired, completely hands-off. Sensors in every room that adjust the airflow based on body heat and occupancy. Sounds great on paper, right? But the programming on the main control board was a complete disaster. 

The system kept defaulting to the overnight cooling cycle right in the middle of the afternoon. You'd have an office full of accountants freezing their tails off in July. I had to get the software engineers out there, and let me tell you, getting those tech guys to actually communicate with my mechanical contractors was like trying to mix oil and water. The tech guys are talking code, my guys are talking ductwork and dampers, and I'm stuck in the middle trying to translate. We had to rip out half the sensor wiring on the third floor just to bypass the main relay. The overtime I had to pay my electricians... man. 

But, uh, anyway. Yeah, the eating. It's just like that automatic system going haywire. I tell myself to stop, but my hands just keep moving.
Do you feel like you're eating at night because you're trying to fill an emotional need or because you feel like you have no control over your actions?

Doc, I gotta ask, are we going in circles here? I feel like I'm repeating myself, but it's exactly what I've been saying. It's not an emotional thing. The whole reason I'm here is because of the control issue. Once I start eating at night, it's like I'm just watching myself do it. I'm telling myself to stop, but my hands just keep going back for more. 

Honestly, you asking me this again reminds me of dealing with the city zoning board. You submit a set of blueprints, right? They kick it back, asking for a revision on the setbacks. You do the revision, stamp it, send it back. A month goes by, and a different clerk asks for the exact same revision because they lost the first one. We had a parking structure project back in '18 where the city made us submit the drainage plan four separate times. Four times! The client was breathing down my neck about the delays, and I'm sitting there at the zoning office trying not to lose my temper at this kid behind the counter who couldn't have been older than twenty-two. He's just blinking at me, talking about 'standard procedure.' Standard procedure my foot. We ended up having to pour the foundation a month behind schedule, which meant we hit the rainy season. And let me tell you, trying to cure concrete in a downpour is a whole other nightmare. You gotta tent the whole site, bring in industrial heaters, pay the crew double-time just to stand around in the mud... 

But anyway, yeah. I don't know how else to explain it to you. It's not about an emotional need. I just can't stop my hands once they get going.
Is your nighttime eating something you feel you're doing because you have no control over it, or is it because you're trying to fulfill an emotional need?

Doc, seriously, is there a hidden camera in here or something? Is this a memory test? Because I swear to you, I've answered this exact question three times now. It is not an emotional need. The whole reason I made this appointment is because I have zero control. I sit there, I watch myself eating, my brain is screaming at me to knock it off, but my hands just keep grabbing more food. I really don't know how to make it any clearer for you.

It's honestly like dealing with punch lists at the end of a big build. You walk the site, you put a piece of blue painter's tape next to a bad mud joint or a scuff on the trim. You tell the drywall guys to fix it. Next week, you walk through again, the tape is gone, but the bad joint is still there! They just pulled the tape off and called it a day. So you put another piece of tape on it and tell them again. 

I had this one sub, Tommy, who ran a finishing crew back in the early two-thousands. Great guy to get a beer with, but absolutely useless with details. I must have marked the same uneven seam in this luxury condo lobby five separate times. The developer was this guy from Chicago, wore suits that probably cost more than my truck, and he had an eye like a hawk. He threatened to withhold the final ten percent of our fee over this one stupid seam. I ended up having to fire Tommy's crew on a Friday, bring in a guy from two towns over, and pay him triple time to float the wall properly over a holiday weekend. My wife was furious because we were supposed to take the boat up to the lake... 

But look, I'm getting off track. My point is, I feel like I'm putting blue tape on the same wall for you here, doc. I'm telling you the exact same thing again. It's not my emotions. It's the control. I just can't stop my hands once they start.

Guilty? Oh, absolutely. The guilt is... it's heavy. It hits me the next morning, usually when I'm standing there looking at the empty wrappers and the dirty dishes piled up in the sink. I just feel this overwhelming shame, like, "How did I let this happen again?" It's embarrassing, really. 

It kind of feels like that time I accidentally backed my truck into my neighbor's mailbox. It was a Saturday morning, early, maybe 6 AM. I was heading out to the hardware store because I was building this birdhouse for my granddaughter. She loves those little yellow finches, you know? Anyway, I wasn't paying attention, just thinking about whether I needed 2-inch or 3-inch screws, and crunch. Backed right into Tom's beautiful brick mailbox. He had just built it himself the summer before. Took him three weekends. I had to go knock on his door, wake him up, and tell him I smashed it. The look on his face... he was wearing this faded blue bathrobe, and he just stared at me. I felt terrible, just completely awful. I ended up paying to have a mason come out and rebuild the whole thing, cost me a pretty penny, but it was the right thing to do. Tom and I are still good friends, actually. We go fishing down at the lake sometimes. Caught a beautiful largemouth bass last spring, must have been five pounds. But yeah, that feeling of standing on his porch, knowing I messed up and having to face the consequences... that's exactly how I feel the morning after I eat all that food. Just ashamed and kicking myself for not paying attention.

Distressed... yeah, I guess you could say that. It's more like this weird out-of-body feeling, really. What brings me in is that once I start eating at night, it feels like I can see myself doing it. I had him on the mini-excavator just doing some light trenching for a sprinkler system on a residential job. I told him, "Jimmy, watch out for the main water line, it runs right along the property edge." I'm standing there drinking my coffee, and I see him swinging the bucket right toward where I know the pipe is. I'm yelling at him to stop, waving my hands, but he's got his ear protection on and he's just staring at the dirt. Boom. Snapped a PVC pipe clean in half. Water shot up like Old Faithful, right into the neighbor's prize-winning rose bushes. The lady came out screaming in her curlers. We had to shut off the water to the whole block for three hours. 

I ended up having to buy her a gift card to the local nursery to smooth things over. They have these really beautiful Japanese maples there, actually. I've been thinking about putting one in my front yard, maybe near the driveway. The leaves turn this incredible deep crimson in the fall. You have to make sure the soil drainage is right, though, or the roots will rot. I've got clay soil, so I'd probably have to amend it with some peat moss and sand... but anyway, yeah, that feeling of watching something happen and not being able to stop it, even when you're shouting at yourself to stop... that's exactly what it's like when I'm in the kitchen at night. My hands just won't listen to my brain.

Pleasure? Hmm... no, not really. I mean, maybe for the first bite or two, but after that, it's just... it's just shoveling it in. There's no real enjoyment to it. It's not like sitting down to a nice meal, you know? 

Speaking of nice meals, my wife and I went to this incredible Italian place downtown for our anniversary last week. Little hole in the wall, you'd miss it if you weren't looking for it. They make all their pasta from scratch right there in the window. I had this veal saltimbocca that was just out of this world. The prosciutto was sliced so thin you could practically see through it, and the sage... man, the sage was so fresh. We had this bottle of Chianti with it, a 2015, I think. The waiter, this older gentleman named Giuseppe, told us all about the vineyard it came from. Apparently, the soil there has a lot of limestone, which gives the grapes this really distinct mineral quality. It got me thinking about the soil on this new commercial project we're bidding on out past the interstate. The core samples came back showing a ton of limestone bedrock, which means we're going to have to bring in the heavy duty drills just to set the foundation pylons. It's going to blow the equipment budget sky high if we don't plan it right. I was telling my lead engineer, Dave, that we need to factor in at least another week of drilling time, but Dave... well, Dave's a bit stubborn. He thinks we can just power through it with the standard rigs. I told him, "Dave, you're gonna burn out the motors on those things before you get ten feet down." But anyway, no, I wouldn't say I enjoy eating all that food at night. It's just something I do.

Stressed or upset? Well... I don't really know. I haven't really noticed a pattern like that, to be honest. It's not like I have a bad day and immediately think, "I need to go eat." It just sort of happens. 

Though, speaking of stress, the supply chain issues lately have been an absolute nightmare. Just last week, I was trying to source some structural steel for a warehouse expansion we're doing out in the industrial park. Usually, I can get a shipment in three, maybe four days tops. I called my guy at the supplier—Bill, I've known him for twenty years, our kids played Little League together—and he tells me it's going to be six weeks. Six weeks! I said, "Bill, I've got a crew of twenty guys standing around with their hands in their pockets, I can't wait six weeks." He just sighed and said it was stuck on some cargo ship out in the Pacific. 

It reminded me of this documentary I watched the other night about the Panama Canal. Fascinating stuff, really. The engineering that went into building those locks back in the early 1900s... they had to excavate something like 200 million cubic yards of earth. And the disease! Malaria and yellow fever were just wiping out the workforce. They finally figured out it was the mosquitoes, so they started draining the swamps and putting oil on the standing water. It's amazing what we can accomplish when we actually understand the root cause of a problem, you know? 

Like my buddy's classic Mustang. It's a '67, cherry red. Beautiful car. But it kept stalling out at stoplights. He took it to three different mechanics, spent a fortune on new spark plugs, a new alternator, the works. Still stalling. Finally, he brings it over to my garage, and we pop the hood. I take one look at the carburetor, and I see the float is sticking. Five minutes and a can of carb cleaner later, she's purring like a kitten. Sometimes it's just the simplest little thing that throws the whole system out of whack. But anyway, what were we talking about? Oh, right, stress. Yeah, I don't really think I eat because I'm upset. It doesn't feel connected to that.

doctor.intent: determine if the patient's nighttime eating is a compulsive behavior
doctor.question: Do you feel like you're compelled to continue eating once you start at night, even if you're not hungry anymore?

target_item.name: Loss_of_Control
target_item.manifestation: What brings me in is that once I start eating at night, it feels like I can see myself doing it and telling myself to stop, but my hands just keep going back for more.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if I feel compelled to continue eating even when not hungry, which directly addresses the sense of lack of control over eating during the episode.

patient.answer:
Yeah, compelled... that's a good word for it. Like I mentioned earlier, that's really the whole reason I'm here. Once I start eating at night, hunger doesn't even factor into it anymore. It feels like I can literally see myself doing it, and I'm standing there in my head telling myself to stop, but my hands just keep going back for more anyway. The brakes are just completely gone. 

It actually reminds me a lot of a continuous concrete pour on a big commercial site. Once you start pouring a massive foundation, you are fully committed. You absolutely cannot stop, no matter what happens. If you stop, the concrete starts to cure unevenly, and you get what we call a cold joint, which completely ruins the structural integrity of the whole slab. I managed this one job back in, oh, must have been 2008 or so... building a five-story parking structure downtown. We had cement trucks lined up around the block, pouring non-stop for fourteen hours straight. Right in the middle of it, the skies just opened up. Absolute torrential downpour. We had guys slipping in the mud, scrambling to get tarps over the exposed rebar, just total chaos. But you can't just tell the trucks to stop. You're compelled to finish the pour, or you lose the whole foundation. 

My site supervisor for that job, Frank, he actually retired right after that project. Said his blood pressure couldn't take the stress anymore. He bought himself one of those big Class A motorhomes and drove out to Arizona with his wife. He sends me pictures sometimes. Says the dry heat does wonders for his arthritis. I've looked into getting an RV myself, actually. Maybe one of those vintage Airstreams. You know, the silver bullets? The aerodynamics on those things are incredible, the way they designed the aluminum shell to reduce drag when you're towing it down the highway. You'd need a heavy-duty truck to pull it, though, probably a three-quarter ton at least with a good towing package. 

But anyway... yeah, once I start eating, it's just like that concrete pour. I just can't stop my hands from going back for more, even when I know the tank is full.

doctor.intent: determine if the eating behavior is a habitual response to emotional states

patient.answer:
Calm and relaxed? Well... I'm really not sure. I haven't noticed if being relaxed would change things, to be honest. I don't even know if I've been completely calm in years. I guess the last time I felt truly relaxed was when my brother and I went up to his cabin near Lake George a couple of summers ago. Beautiful spot. Pine trees everywhere, right on the water. We were supposed to just be fishing and kicking back, but you know me, I can't just sit still. I took one look at his back deck and told him the support joists were completely rotted out. I mean, it was a major safety hazard. You get a heavy snowfall up there, or get a few guys standing on it with a grill, and that whole structure is coming down. 

So instead of fishing, we spent three days driving back and forth to the lumber yard, buying pressure-treated wood, pulling up all the old boards... I actually prefer using composite decking nowadays on my projects. Trex, or something like that. It costs a bit more upfront, but the maintenance is basically zero. You don't have to stain it, it doesn't splinter. My neighbor, Tom, he put in a traditional cedar deck a few years ago, and he's out there every single summer power washing and resealing the thing. Seems like a massive waste of a weekend to me. Sundays are for watching the game or tinkering in the garage, not inhaling wood stain fumes, you know? He uses this oil-based stuff that just smells awful, wafts right over the fence into my yard... 

But wait, what were we talking about? Oh, right, eating when I'm calm. Yeah, I really couldn't tell you. I just haven't paid attention to whether being relaxed would stop me from doing it. I'm just not sure.

doctor.intent: determine if the patient's nighttime eating is related to emotional states
doctor.question: Do you think your nighttime eating is triggered by feelings of emotional upset or stress?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the nighttime eating is triggered by emotional upset or stress, which is not covered by any of the symptoms in the patient's profile.

patient.answer:
Triggered by stress or being upset? I... well, I don't really think so. I haven't noticed any kind of connection like that, to be honest. It's not like I get mad and then head straight for the kitchen. 

Though, you know, speaking of stress and triggers... the stress testing we have to do on load-bearing steel columns, now *that* is something. We send these material samples out to an independent lab, and they put them under these massive hydraulic presses to test the tensile strength. They just keep dialing up the pressure, thousands and thousands of pounds, until the steel finally buckles. When it gives, the sound it makes... it's like a cannon going off right next to your head. My old site foreman, Dave, he used to run a testing facility down in Scranton before he came to work for me. Stubborn guy. Refused to wear the heavy-duty ear protection because he said it messed up the way his hard hat fit. I told him, "Dave, nobody cares what your hair looks like on a job site." But he wouldn't listen. Now he wears two hearing aids and can barely hear his wife when she's sitting right next to him. 

She's a nice lady, actually. Makes this incredible baked ziti. They brought a huge aluminum pan of it to the company picnic last summer. We had it out at that state park, the one with the big timber pavilion. The roof on that pavilion, though... just terrible craftsmanship. I was looking up at the trusses while we were eating, and you could see they used the completely wrong gauge gusset plates for the joints. One heavy winter snowstorm and that whole roof is coming down on somebody's head. It's a liability nightmare waiting to happen. 

But, uh, anyway... what were you asking? Emotional stress? Yeah, no, I don't really see a pattern there with the eating. I just haven't noticed it being triggered by my mood or anything like that.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's nighttime eating is a habitual behavior
doctor.question: Do you find yourself eating at night out of habit, even when you're not thinking about food or feeling hungry?

patient.answer:
Habit? You know, I'm not really sure if it's a habit or not. I haven't really thought about it that way. I mean, I guess I don't really know if I'm thinking about food or not when it happens. 

But speaking of habits, you wouldn't believe the habits some of these subcontractors have on the job site. It's enough to drive you up the wall. Take my electrical guy, for instance. Great guy, knows his stuff, but he has this habit of leaving his wire clippings just scattered everywhere. I mean, everywhere. You walk into a room he's been working in, and it looks like a copper wire explosion. I tell him, "Look, it takes two seconds to sweep that up, and it's a major safety hazard." You get a guy walking through there in work boots, he slips on a piece of Romex, and suddenly I'm dealing with a worker's comp claim and a delayed schedule. 

And schedules, let me tell you, that's another thing. People just don't respect the timeline anymore. Back when I started in this business, if you said you were going to be on-site at 7:00 AM, you were there at 6:45, drinking coffee and ready to go. Now? You're lucky if the drywall crew shows up by 9:00, and half the time they're missing a guy because his truck broke down. I actually had to buy a backup generator for a site last month because the local utility company was dragging their feet on getting the temporary power pole set up. Cost me an arm and a leg, but you can't just have guys standing around waiting for the lights to turn on. Time is money in this business, you know? 

But, uh, what were we talking about? Habit? Yeah, I don't know. I really couldn't say if I'm doing it out of habit or not. I just haven't paid that much attention to it.

patient.answer:
If someone took all the food out? Well, I... I guess I'm not really sure if I'd notice right away. I haven't really thought about a situation like that.

We were pulling down the lath and plaster in the dining room—which is a nightmare of a job, by the way, the dust gets absolutely everywhere, into your lungs, your eyes, even with the masks on. Anyway, we opened up this one wall, and the space between the studs was completely packed with old glass bottles. Hundreds of them. Medicine bottles, liquor bottles, some of them still had corks in them. 

My demo guy, Ricky, he thought we'd struck gold. He started talking about how antique bottles go for big money on eBay. He spent his entire lunch break carefully pulling them out and lining them up on the front porch. I had to tell him, "Ricky, we're not running an antique shop here, we have a framing inspection on Thursday and you're holding up the plumbers." The plumbers on that job were a whole other headache. They wanted to run the main stack right through the middle of where the new kitchen island was supposed to go. I had to sit down with the blueprints and show them—literally trace it with my finger—how we could reroute it through the old butler's pantry so we wouldn't ruin the open concept layout the client was paying top dollar for. You really have to hold these guys' hands sometimes, I swear. 

But, uh, what did you ask me? About noticing if the food was gone? Yeah, I don't know. I really couldn't tell you if I'd notice or not. I just haven't given it any thought.

Coping with my emotions? I... I really couldn't say. I don't think I'm doing it to manage my feelings or anything like that. I just haven't noticed any kind of connection there. 

Speaking of managing emotions, though... if you want to see some real emotions, you should try managing a commercial build for a first-time restaurant owner. I'm running a job downtown right now, retrofitting this beautiful old bank building into an upscale steakhouse. I had to pull him aside and say, "Look, buddy, crying over brass isn't going to get your certificate of occupancy signed any faster." 

I mean, the real issue wasn't even the lights, it was the HVAC system. The original ductwork in that bank was from the 1970s, completely inadequate for a commercial kitchen exhaust. We had to bring in a crane to drop a massive new makeup air unit onto the roof. Coordinating a street closure downtown for a 50-ton crane? Now *that* requires some serious management. You have to deal with the city permitting office, and let me tell you, those bureaucrats move at the speed of molasses. I spent three hours on hold with the Department of Transportation just to get a traffic control plan approved. And then the flaggers they sent out didn't even bring the right detour signs. It was a complete circus. 

But, uh... sorry, I lost my train of thought there. You were asking about my emotions? Yeah, I don't really know about that. I just don't think I'm eating to cope with anything. I haven't felt like that's the reason at all.

target_item.name: Loss_of_Control

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about feeling an overwhelming urge to eat even if I don't want to, which corresponds to a sense of lack of control over eating.

patient.answer:
An overwhelming urge... yeah. Actually, that's really what brings me in here. It's exactly like that. Once I start eating at night, it feels like I'm just watching myself do it. I'm sitting there, literally telling myself in my head to stop, but my hands just keep going back for more. I just can't stop them. 

It's almost like a concrete pour, honestly. Once you start a pour, there is absolutely no stopping it. You ever been on a site during a massive foundation pour? Once those mixer trucks are lined up down the block and the pump truck is primed, that's it. You can't just hit pause. We had this one job a couple years back, a huge custom build out by the lake. We were right in the middle of pouring the retaining walls, and the skies just opened up. Torrential downpour. The client's architect—this kid fresh out of school who didn't know a trowel from a hole in the ground—starts screaming at us to stop the pour.
